definition: Providing feedback on intermediate steps rather than only final outcomes.
example: Score individual reasoning steps.
caveat: Step labels can be costly and themselves ambiguous.

definition: Compressing vectors by splitting them into subspaces and encoding each with a learned codebook.
example: Reduce approximate-search memory.
caveat: Compression introduces distance-estimation error.

definition: Input content supplied to condition a model's output.
example: Provide a task instruction and relevant context.
caveat: A prompt can include more than visible user text.

definition: Connecting several model calls so one call's output informs the next.
example: Extract facts, then draft, then check a response.
caveat: A fixed chain is not necessarily an autonomous agent.

definition: Designing input instructions, examples, and formatting to influence model behavior without ordinary weight updates.
example: Add a clear task specification and output schema.
caveat: Not the same as training soft prompts or fine-tuning.

definition: Combining outputs across different prompts or prompt formulations.
example: Aggregate predictions from several templates.
caveat: Prompt variants may produce highly correlated errors.

definition: Instructions embedded in lower-trust input that attempt to override intended system behavior or authority boundaries.
example: A retrieved document tries to redirect an assistant.
caveat: Malicious content can arrive through tools, files, or user input.

definition: Variation in model behavior caused by semantically minor changes in input wording or formatting.
example: Test a benchmark under paraphrased instructions.
caveat: One favorable prompt can overstate reliability.

definition: Learning continuous prompt embeddings while freezing most or all model weights.
example: Adapt a model with trainable virtual tokens.
caveat: Different from manually writing a better text prompt.

definition: Tracking changes to prompts, templates, and associated configuration as identifiable artifacts.
example: Compare two production instruction templates.
caveat: Identical prompts can behave differently with changed models or tools.

definition: A measurable substitute for a harder-to-measure real objective.
example: Use a judge score as a proxy for usefulness.
caveat: A correlated proxy can fail under strong optimization.

definition: Removing model components to reduce complexity or resource use.
example: Remove weak tree branches or neural weights.
caveat: Tree pruning and neural pruning use different mechanisms.

definition: Using model predictions as training labels for unlabeled examples.
example: Label high-confidence examples for semi-supervised training.
caveat: Confident mistakes can be amplified.

definition: A generalized inverse used even when a matrix is rectangular or singular.
example: Solve a least-squares system.
caveat: It does not make an ill-conditioned problem harmless.

definition: A tensor-computation and automatic-differentiation framework used to build and train machine-learning models.
example: Implement a custom neural network.
caveat: Framework choice does not determine model quality.

definition: Expected return after taking a particular action and then following a policy.
example: Score possible moves before selecting one.
caveat: Q values are not necessarily probabilities.

definition: An off-policy value-learning method using a greedy next-action target.
example: Learn action values from exploratory experience.
caveat: Function approximation can introduce instability.

definition: Fine-tuning LoRA adapters while a frozen base model is held in a low-bit representation, commonly using 4-bit quantization.
example: Adapt a larger model within a smaller memory budget.
caveat: Quantized storage does not imply all arithmetic uses four-bit precision.

definition: Growth proportional to the square of a problem-size variable, up to asymptotic constants.
example: Describe dense attention interactions as sequence length increases.
caveat: The relevant variable and measured resource must be specified.

definition: A classifier using class-specific Gaussian covariance estimates, producing quadratic boundaries.
example: Model classes with different covariance patterns.
caveat: Covariance estimation needs enough data.

definition: A threshold below which a specified fraction of a distribution or sample lies.
example: Report a prediction interval using lower and upper quantiles.
caveat: Finite-sample interpolation conventions can produce slightly different quantiles.

definition: Estimating conditional quantiles instead of only a conditional mean.
example: Predict a high-demand quantile for capacity planning.
caveat: Separate fitted quantiles may cross without constraints.

definition: Representing values with a smaller or constrained numerical set to reduce resource requirements.
example: Store weights using low-bit representations.
caveat: Memory savings do not guarantee speedups on all hardware.

definition: A factor mapping between quantized integer-like values and represented real values.
example: Convert int8 values back to approximate weights.
caveat: Scale granularity affects both overhead and accuracy.

definition: Training while simulating or accounting for quantization effects.
example: Prepare a model for low-precision deployment.
caveat: Training operations often still use higher precision internally.

definition: An optimizer approximating curvature rather than computing the full Hessian each step.
example: Use L-BFGS for smooth parameter fitting.
caveat: Approximate curvature can become unreliable with noisy gradients.

definition: A vector representing what information an attention position is seeking.
example: Compare one token's query with available keys.
caveat: Unrelated to a database query except by analogy.

definition: Adding related terms or alternate formulations to improve retrieval coverage.
example: Include synonyms in lexical search.
caveat: Expansion can reduce precision by introducing irrelevant matches.

definition: Transforming a query to better express the retrieval need.
example: Resolve a follow-up question into a standalone query.
caveat: A rewrite can accidentally change the user's intent.

definition: A regression score comparing residual squared error with a reference variation around the target mean.
example: Compare fit against a mean-prediction baseline.
caveat: Out-of-sample R² can be negative.

definition: A kernel based on an exponential of negative squared distance.
example: Model smooth nonlinear decision boundaries.
caveat: Its bandwidth determines how local the similarity is.

definition: A bagged tree ensemble adding random feature selection at splits.
example: Predict from mixed tabular features.
caveat: Feature importance can be biased or misleading.

definition: Random features approximating suitable shift-invariant kernels via sampled frequencies.
example: Approximate an RBF kernel with a linear model.
caveat: The kernel's spectral distribution determines sampling.

definition: Sampling hyperparameter configurations from chosen distributions.
example: Explore learning rates on a log scale.
caveat: The search distribution is an important design choice.

definition: A value initializing a pseudorandom generator for reproducible sampling.
example: Record seeds for data splits and weight initialization.
caveat: One seed does not control all hardware or library nondeterminism.

definition: A numerical quantity whose value depends on a random outcome.
example: Treat a sampled class label as a random variable.
caveat: Random variables are mathematical mappings, not just stored numbers.

definition: An experiment assigning treatments randomly to reduce confounding.
example: Randomize users between two model variants.
caveat: Interference, attrition, and implementation errors can still bias results.

definition: A LoRA variant using a scaling rule designed to remain effective at higher adapter ranks.
example: Train higher-rank adapters more stably.
caveat: It changes scaling, not the low-rank update structure itself.

definition: Ordering items by predicted relevance, preference, or utility.
example: Rank documents for a search query.
caveat: Good classification accuracy does not guarantee good ranking.

definition: Repeatedly fitting candidate models to small subsets and retaining a model supported by many inliers.
example: Fit geometry despite mismatched points.
caveat: It requires a meaningful inlier threshold and enough clean data.

definition: An agent pattern interleaving generated reasoning-related steps, actions, and observations.
example: Iterate between planning and tool results.
caveat: A generated rationale is not proof of a faithful internal explanation.

definition: Intermediate generated steps used or presented during problem solving.
example: Store a sequence of calculations before a final answer.
caveat: A plausible trace can be incorrect or post-hoc.

definition: The fraction of actual positive cases correctly identified.
example: Measure how many target events are detected.
caveat: High recall can coexist with many false positives.

definition: The fraction of relevant items recovered among the top k results under a specified relevance set.
example: Check whether retrieval captures supporting evidence.
caveat: Some benchmarks use a hit-style convention instead; report the definition.

definition: The input region that can influence a particular unit or output position.
example: Estimate how much image context a neuron uses.
caveat: The effective influence can be much narrower than the theoretical region.

definition: Combining ranked lists using scores based on reciprocal rank plus a stabilizing constant.
example: Merge lexical and dense search results.
caveat: Rank fusion ignores the absolute calibration of original scores.

definition: Predicting items or actions likely to interest a user or context.
example: Suggest relevant products or articles.
caveat: Feedback loops can distort future training data.

definition: A loss comparing reconstructed data with the original input or target.
example: Train an autoencoder to reproduce inputs.
caveat: Low reconstruction loss need not imply useful semantics.

definition: A generative transport approach that learns approximately straight trajectories between paired source and target samples.
example: Reduce the complexity of generative sampling trajectories.
caveat: Straight training paths do not guarantee exact one-step sampling.

definition: A network processing a sequence through a repeatedly updated hidden state.
example: Model a time series one step at a time.
caveat: Long-range credit assignment can be difficult.
